'''David Botstein''' (September 8, 1942 – February 27, 2026) was an American biologist. He was the director of the Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics at [[Princeton University]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.molbio2.princeton.edu/index.php?option=content&task=view&id=201 |title=Princeton University - Department of Molecular Biology - David Botstein |access-date=November 8, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061127033459/http://www.molbio2.princeton.edu/index.php?option=content&task=view&id=201 |archive-date=November 27, 2006 }} David Botstein at Princeton Department of Molecular Biology</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=History |url=https://lsi.princeton.edu/about/history |access-date=March 21, 2026 |website=Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics}}</ref><ref name=interview>{{Cite interview |last=Botstein|first=David|interviewer-last=Gitschier | interviewer-first=Jane | title = Willing to Do the Math: An Interview with David Botstein| doi = 10.1371/journal.pgen.0020079 | journal = PLOS Genetics | volume = 2 | issue = 5 | article-number = e79 | year = 2006 | pmid =  16733551| pmc =1464829 | doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailyprincetonian.com/archives/2005/10/18/news/13503.shtml |title=The Daily Princetonian - Mapping the path of genetics |access-date=2006-10-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061020012122/http://www.dailyprincetonian.com/archives/2005/10/18/news/13503.shtml |archive-date=2006-10-20 }} The Daily Princetonian – Mapping the path of genetics</ref> from 2003 to 2013 and was the Anthony B. Evnin Professor of Genomics. From 2013 to 2023, he was the founding [[Chief Science Officer]] of [[Calico (company)|Calico]], a biotechnology company with a focus on the [[biology of aging]] to devise interventions to enable people to lead longer and healthier lives.<ref name="Mast2023">{{cite news |last1=Mast |first1=Jason |title=Calico looking for new chief scientist after celebrated biologist David Botstein quietly retires |url=https://www.statnews.com/2023/01/24/calico-chief-scientist-david-botstein-retires/ |access-date=2 August 2025 |work=[[Stat (website)|STAT News]] |date=January 24, 2023}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
David Botsztejn was born in Zurich, Switzerland on September 8, 1942. His parents, Chaim and Anna Botsztejn (later Charles and Anne Botstein), were Jewish research physicians from Poland, his father a radiation oncologist and his mother a pediatrician.<ref name="interview" /> In 1949, the family emigrated to the United States, where their surname was changed to Botstein.<ref name="kolata" /> 

Botstein graduated from the [[Bronx High School of Science]] in 1959, and [[Harvard University]] in 1963.<ref name=":0">{{Cite Q|Q141250742}}</ref> He started his Ph.D. work under [[Maurice Sanford Fox]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], then moved and received a [[Ph.D.]] from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1967 for work on [[P22 phage]].<ref name="botstein">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=David|last=Botstein |title=The Synthesis and Maturation of Phage-P22 DNA |publisher=University of Michigan |date=1967 |author-link=David Botstein|id={{ProQuest|302261666}}}}</ref>

==Career==
Botstein taught at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where he became a professor of genetics. Botstein joined [[Genentech]], Inc. in 1987 as vice president – science. In 1990, he became chairman of the Department of Genetics at [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":0" /> Botstein was elected to the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] in 1981 and to the [[Institute of Medicine]] in 1993.

He was the director of the Integrated Science Program at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Thean|first=Tara|title=Integrated Science Pays Off for Graduates|url=http://www.dailyprincetonian.com/2009/10/12/24100/|work=The Daily Princetonian|publisher=Princeton University Press|access-date=October 23, 2011|archive-date=August 30, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110830154320/http://www.dailyprincetonian.com/2009/10/12/24100/}}</ref>

In 1980, Botstein and his colleagues Ray White, Mark Skolnick, and [[Ronald W. Davis]] proposed a method<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Botstein | first1 = D.
| last2 = White | first2 = R.
| last3 = Skolnick | first3 = M.
| last4 = Davis | first4 = R.
| title = Construction of a genetic linkage map in man using restriction fragment length polymorphisms
| journal = American Journal of Human Genetics
| volume = 32
| issue = 3
| pages = 314–331
| year = 1980
| pmid = 6247908
| pmc = 1686077
}}</ref> for constructing a [[genetic linkage]] map using [[restriction fragment length polymorphism]]s that was used in subsequent years to identify several human disease genes including [[Huntington's disease|Huntington's]] and [[BRCA1]]. Variations of this method were used in the mapping efforts that predated and enabled the sequencing phase of the [[Human Genome Project]].

In 1998, Botstein and his postdoctoral fellow [[Michael Eisen]], together with graduate student Paul Spellman and colleague [[Patrick O. Brown|Patrick Brown]], developed a statistical method and graphical interface that is widely used to interpret genomic data including [[microarray]] data.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Eisen | first1 = M.
| author-link1 = Michael Eisen
| last2 = Spellman | first2 = P.
| last3 = Brown | first3 = P.
| author-link3 = Patrick O. Brown
| last4 = Botstein | first4 = D.
| author-link4 = David Botstein
| title = Cluster analysis and display of genome-wide expression patterns
| journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
| volume = 95
| issue = 25
| pages = 14863–14868
| year = 1998
| pmid = 9843981
| pmc = 24541 | doi=10.1073/pnas.95.25.14863
| bibcode = 1998PNAS...9514863E
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> This approach was refined and applied for diverse applications, including for a molecular classification of heterogenous tumors using gene expression. These efforts included work on discovery of tumor subtypes with [[Lou Staudt]], [[Ash Alizadeh]] and [[Ronald Levy (scientist)|Ronald Levy]], yielding a refined classification of [[Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma|diffuse large B cell lymphomas]], and in painting the molecular portraits for refined classification of [[Breast cancer classification|breast cancers]] with [[Anne-Lise Børresen-Dale]] and Charles Perou. He has subsequently worked on the creation of the influential [[Gene Ontology]]<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Botstein | first1 = D. | author-link1 = David Botstein| last2 = Cherry | first2 = J. M. | last3 = Ashburner | first3 = M. | author-link3 = Michael Ashburner| last4 = Ball | first4 = C. A. | last5 = Blake | first5 = J. A. | last6 = Butler | first6 = H. | last7 = Davis | first7 = A. P. | last8 = Dolinski | first8 = K. | last9 = Dwight | first9 = S. S. | last10 = Eppig | first10 = J. T. | last11 = Harris | first11 = M. A. | last12 = Hill | first12 = D. P. | last13 = Issel-Tarver | first13 = L. | last14 = Kasarskis | first14 = A. | last15 = Lewis | first15 = S. | author-link15 = Suzanna Lewis| last16 = Matese | first16 = J. C. | last17 = Richardson | first17 = J. E. | last18 = Ringwald | first18 = M. | last19 = Rubin | first19 = G. M. | author-link19 = Gerald M. Rubin| last20 = Sherlock | first20 = G. | title = Gene ontology: Tool for the unification of biology. The Gene Ontology Consortium | journal = [[Nature Genetics]] | volume = 25 | issue = 1 | pages = 25–29 | doi = 10.1038/75556 | year = 2000 | pmid = 10802651 | pmc =3037419 }} {{open access}}</ref> with [[Michael Ashburner]] and [[Suzanna Lewis]]. He was one of the founding editors of the journal ''[[Molecular Biology of the Cell]]'', along with [[Erkki Ruoslahti]] and [[Keith Yamamoto]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.molbiolcell.org/site/misc/edboard.xhtml|title= MBC Editorial Board}}</ref>

In 2013, Botstein was named chief scientific officer of [[Google]]'s [[anti-aging]] health startup [[Calico (company)|Calico]].

==Personal life and death==
Botstein was an alumnus of [[Camp Rising Sun (New York)|Camp Rising Sun]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}} He was the brother of the conductor [[Leon Botstein]] and of the pediatric cardiologist Eva Botstein Griepp.<ref name="kolata" /><ref name=interview />

Botstein died in Palo Alto, California, on February 27, 2026, at the age of 83.<ref name="kolata">{{Cite news |last=Kolata |first=Gina |date=March 20, 2026 |title=David Botstein, Gene-Mapping Pioneer, Dies at 83 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/20/science/david-botstein-dead.html |access-date=March 21, 2026 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David Botstein |url=https://www.online-tribute.com/DavidBotstein |website=Online Tribute |access-date=1 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

His cause of death was Parkinson's disease at an assisted living facility.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kolata |first=Gina |date=2026-03-20 |title=David Botstein, Gene-Mapping Pioneer, Dies at 83 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/20/science/david-botstein-dead.html |access-date=2026-09-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==Awards==
Botstein has won the [[Eli Lilly and Company-Elanco Research Award|Eli Lilly and Company Award in Microbiology]] (1978), the Genetics Society of America Medal (1988, with [[Ira Herskowitz]]),<ref name="genemedal"/> the [[William Allan Award|Allan Award]] of the [[American Society of Human Genetics]] (1989, with [[Raymond L. White|Ray White]]), the [[Gruber Prize in Genetics]] (2003), the [[Albany Medical Center Prize]] (2010, with [[Eric Lander]] and [[Francis Collins]]), and the [[Dan David Prize]] in 2012. In 2013, he was awarded the $3 million [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]] for his work and in 2020 the [[Thomas Hunt Morgan Medal]] of the [[Genetics Society of America]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://genestogenomes.org/congratulations-to-the-recipients-of-the-2020-gsa-awards/|title=Congratulations to the recipients of the 2020 GSA Awards!|date=January 29, 2020|publisher=Genetics Society of America|access-date=February 5, 2020|website=Genes to Genomes}}</ref> In 2016, [[Semantic Scholar]] AI program included Botstein on its list of most top ten most influential biomedical researchers.<ref>{{Cite web|first=Dalmeet|last=Singh|date=2017-10-17|title=Who's the most influential biomedical scientist? Computer program guided by artificial intelligence says it knows|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/who-s-most-influential-biomedical-scientist-computer-program-guided-artificial|access-date=2020-09-22|website=Science {{!}} AAAS|language=en}}</ref>
